summary: David Tillotson, as President of the Milwaukee Audubon Society, strongly opposes ORV use on federal public lands, arguing that the Draft Environmental Impact Statement improperly institutionalizes and legitimizes ORV activity rather than questioning whether such use should be permitted at all. He contends that ORVs cause documented ecological damage, destroy wilderness solitude and atmosphere, threaten endangered species, and that the multiple-use concept cannot reconcile wilderness values with ORV use. He calls for a phasing out of motorized vehicles from public lands, limiting ORV activity to private lands, and urges federal managers to use the word 'no' rather than accommodating ever-expanding ORV encroachment.

statement.text:
14 Mar 1973
Mr. Nathaniel Reed US Department of Interior Washington, D.C. 20340
Dear Mr. Reed,
Attached is a position paper of the Milwaukee Audubon Society dealing with the subject of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land.
It is our understanding that public reaction was invited to a draft statement on ORV use issued by one of Interior's subagencies - the Eureau of Outdoor Recreation.
We trust that you will see that our position on the ORV matter gets to the proper agency in time for the hearing on this matter.
Sincerely
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society
12259 Underwood Fkwy
Wauwatosa, Wis 53226
CC: Cynthia Wilson (Natl Audubon)
CC: Ed Brigham (Natl Midwest Audubon Rep)
114
3/27/1

Position Paper
Milwaukee Audubon Society
regarding
The Use of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land
prepared by
David Tillotson
President
Milwaukee Audubon Society
12 March 1973
In our assessment of the Draft Impact Statement on Off The Road Recreational Vehicles (prepared by the Department of Interior to implement Presidential Executive Order #11644) we believe that one serious weakness immediately presents itself. This is the fact that the Department of Interior Draft Statement helps institutionalize motorized recreational vehicles on the public lands and waters. It appears to make proper and acceptable what we in the Audubon Society believe is improper and un-acceptable. Before we as a Nation decide on THERE to use the ORV's schould we not decide THETHER to use them?
We seriously challenge and question the environmental wisdom in conceding to the thought that ORV's really belong, in almost any setting, on Federal Lands.

In a time of fast diminishing recreational space, is it wise to give any Governmental help (by an ORV policy statement) to ORV's, that simply by their existance and normal method of operation shrink recreational space at a disproportionately rapid rate. One can hear the motors for miles. The outdoor atmosphere is spoiled and diluted. ORV's swallow up land in minutes that would take a hiker hours to traverse. The new recreational vehicles are simply sophisticated ways for exploiting untouched nature more rapidly. Their growing use and popularity fits neatly, we will admit, into our current environmental milieu which is quite frankly hedonistic and materialistic.
The draft statement by implying that since the vehicles are here and are now using Public Lands, that it is proper for such use to continue without challenge.
Our second objection is that the statement as it stands is conciliatory and even not neutral in that it more or less takes the position of the ORV manufacturer and user by saying that this or that use MAY harm the soil, MIGHT damage lakes, etc, etc. In point of fact there are numerous documented instances where lakes, forests, waters, lands and wildlife are actually being harmed.
To mention just a few:
1. Trout spawning area spoiled by motorcycles in Sequoia Natl Forest (Calif) Documented Audubon Mag Jan '72
114. Coyotes run over by snowmobilers in Grand Teton Park (Wyo) Documented Audubon Mag Jan 172 
3. Snow compaction (in Canada) injures microenvironment of small mammals shrinking food chains Aud Mag Jan '72

4. Motorized outdoorsman can cause 200 times more damage to landscapes than the walker Audubon Mag Jan 172
5. Elk & Deer harassment by snowmobiles in S.E. Idaho "drains these animals of as much energy as a week's normal winter existance."

Aud Mag Jan '72
6. A Federal Game manager says that "snowmobiles can harm wild animals by driving them from protective cover & food supplies".

documented Milwaukee Journal Feb 6 '72
7. In Humbolt Natl Forest (Nev) jeeps and ORV's caused $50,000 damage to soil and vegetation. Aud Mag Jan 172
8. In one BLM study area in the west, trail bikers stripped away 60% of the vegetation in a 1500 acre area Aud Mag Jan 172
We question the unsubstantiated statement in the draft that a snowmobile or other ORV's are a boost to family ties. Considering what the car is generally known to have done to the American home and family life - 
_{\rm We}
 challenge the idea that ORV's are going to "Cement family relationships".
It will be argued that tens of thousands of individuals already own ORV's, that it is too late to outlaw on public lands; we can only regulate. We do not concele this point. On private lands, where motors are operated in such fashion that they do not infringe on the legitimate rights of contiguous property owners, we have no argument.
But we do question whether the larger, long term interests of today's and tomorrow's citizens (and ecosystems?) are best served by opening government lands to general use by ORV's.
We believe that the multiple use concept is deformed and abused 114 by asking that it stretch far enough to blanket, simultaneously, wilderness values and values pursued by ORV users.

We question the wisdom of permitting the great wilderness and wildlife sanctuaries (whether "official" or unofficial) to be overwhelmed by ORV activity. We believe the chief value of much undesignated federal land is that it furnishes a valuable staging area, a resting area, a cosmic mood, a wilderness retreat (incidentally for man and primarily for wildlife) and that non-use is healthful and recharges the intricate (not totally known) mechanisms of the various ecosystems. "Unused" wilderness, for example, is responsible for clean water coming out of mountain country as clean as it is.
Stricter controls, stricter enforcement is needed, with the focus on THE SPECIAL KIND OF HARM done to nature by ORV activity. Beyond the obvious damage to plants, lands, and animals and waterways, there is a loss of mood, a loss of authentic outdoor atmosphere which may be far more significant than all other kinds of damage combined.
The "differentness" of the land - the land undominated by ORV's is why we believe a vast majority of outdoor oriented citizens like the out of doors. These are the citizens, many now deceased, who have helped see to it that one third of the land of the United States has remained in public hands and in one sense, still "whole".
We of Audubon feel about all landscapes as Theodore Roosevenlt felt about one landscape, the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. The ages have been at work upon it - let it be.
114 Historian Will Lurant has written that Mations are born stoic and die epicurian. Are the CRV's an example of a mechanized epicurianism? A squandering of all the untouched land in America? Land that has not thus far been defiled by the joyous fact that it is remote?

ORV
ORV's don't give citizens who want to escape into nature the opportunity to do just that. The ORV catches the eye, it dominates the scene with motion, it kills solitude and stunts the growth and development of outdoor aesthetics. Its root is commercial, not esthetic; hedonistic and pagan, not frugal, disciplined, and sacrificial. In other words, the kinds of philosophies that are pre-requisites to the conservation movement are really not yet understood to the ORV user and manufacturer.
Because of the nature of the ORV itself, we must put restraints on it we will not put on other kinds of recreational devices; sail boats, kayaks, canoes, rowboats, bicycles, skis, snowshoes, ice boats. We believe that ORV's (land, water, air) pose very serious threats to several of our endangered species. By means of the ORV we visualize an ever growing number of ill-informed hunters having access to timber wolves, condors, eagles, antelope, prairie dogs, mountain lions. The consequences, for wildlife, of access by way of ORV use, is ominous for the future of many species.
People are coming into nature hopeful of finding enough quality in the way of the environment to save them the extra expense and time of driving a thousand miles more to a place—like a National Fark where severe restrictions have curtailed ORV activity. Much public land, all over the nation, should be free of the blight of the machine.

114 Vast, intact acreages, not subdued by ORV activity, ought to be available to those who are gentler users of the land.

To sum up, we do not believe that certain conflicting uses on ' public lands can be reconciled and no amount of cosmetic rhetoric should be allowed to conceal this fact.
The draft statement, as written, is, in a sense, a commentary on the permissive temper of our times. Rather than ever say NO to anybody, be it the Army Corps of Engineers, the Highways builders, the stream channelizers, the rioters on the campus, or group X,Y, or Z that has siezed a park or a building or a National Forest and then demands that we negotiate. We can't seem to consider the social and environmental imperative of using the simple word, NO!
Merely because Federal managers have thus far (apparently in lieu of directives from anyone) failed to halt the mushrooming encroachments by ORV's on Federal lands, is no reason to assume that the presence of these vehicles is proper or that it should be allowed to continue.
In the absence of a directive, we believe managers should have held the Line and not accommodated the ORV user.
The assumption by Federal land managers that ORV's do BELONG is far more pernicious than one would think. For it leads to institutionalization of the idea that the ORV on Federal land is here to stay.
The land managers are put in a position of accomodating themselves to the CRV and being on the defensive from the beginning.
114 We are convinced that the long suffering but concerned silent majority of the American public gets a great feeling of solace from merely contemplating the fact that vast chunks of Federal land are as yet unspoiled by the Users and producers of ORV's.

And further, that these lands are going to be protected by Federal managers for all time to come, regardless of the talk (and money) of the advocates of motorized exploitation.
In World War II when gas rationing and the war effort cut the visits to the National Forests, there was a 50% drop in the losses due to forest fire. Natural (lightning) fires tend to start high on the mountain while man caused fires (9 out of 10 forest fires are still man caused) start at a lower level and can do much more damage. Thy does the draft statement emphasize the potential of the ORV in preventing fire, when there is historical evidence from World War II and the National Forests, that human access to the forest, especially the remote forests, will increase the number of fires. Come studies that have delved into the psychological make-up of the ORV user indicates that they have a significantly higher accident rate that the non-user. The ORV buff turns out to be a "risk taker" and thus has a higher accident rate. This risk taker is going to pose amever greater threat by fire in the forest and on the grasslands - and game law violators are going to be next to impossible to stop because the ORV will provide opportunity to go anywhere.
114 On most public lands, in such places as the National Parks and monuments, in State Parks, in nearly all the Mational and State Forests, and on the vast tracts controlled by the Bureau of Land Management, we believe motors are a mistake. The evidence of ecological damage and impairment of the natural mood is going to increase, not decrease.

Therefore we believe that a phasing out of the motors from various "established" places should begin at once. We believe that conservation authorities should not develop or promote trails as these trails lead to "locking in" a kind of outdoor use that must eventually be phased out. Also trails are merely "way stations" on the road to ever greater development.
When Congress created the Park System in 1916 it stated that "Above all, the mood of naturalness should prevail."
Except for emergency rescue work, law enforcement activity, and necessary patrols of one kind or another, we believe that concept should eventually govern ORV activity on all public land. Private holdings, private lands, vasts tracts furnished by the manufacturers of the ORV's themselves (two thirds of this Nation's land mass is private) - this is where ORV activity can legitimately be expanded.
Respectfully submitted
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society 12259 Underwood Pkwy Wauwatosa, Wis 53226
